title: AWS ParallelCluster
text:
Deploying the cluster brings everything together. parallelcluster/deploy.sh does the following:

Reads your settings from an env file.
Reads everything else from the Pulumi stack outputs.
Renders the cluster template and the node scripts.
Uploads the scripts to s3://<bucket>/<clustername>/.
Runs pcluster create-cluster.




The Pulumi stack is deployed (Pulumi). Its name is the cluster name.
A custom AMI is built (AMI), unless all sessions run in Apptainer containers (see When you need it).
The ParallelCluster CLI is installed. The version is pinned in the root pyproject.toml:
uv sync                      # in the repository root
source .venv/bin/activate
aws, pulumi, jq and perl are on your PATH.




cd parallelcluster
cp envs/demo.env.example envs/<clustername>.env
$EDITOR envs/<clustername>.env
./deploy.sh envs/<clustername>.env --dry-run   # render and validate only
./deploy.sh envs/<clustername>.env
envs/*.env files are ignored by git, so you can keep one per environment. The settings:



Table 1: Deployment settings









Variable
Meaning




CLUSTERNAME
Cluster name. Must equal the Pulumi stack name.


STACKNAME
Pulumi stack to read from (default: CLUSTERNAME)


REGION
AWS region


AMI
Custom AMI from image/build-image.sh. Empty: official ParallelCluster Ubuntu 24.04 image (needs SINGULARITY_SUPPORT=true).


PWB_VERSION
Posit Workbench version, e.g. 2026.10.0-233.pro1


CONFIG
Cluster template config/cluster-config-wb.<CONFIG>.tmpl: default or easybuild


APPS_EFS_ID
Existing EFS with the EasyBuild stack (CONFIG=easybuild only)


ALLOWEDIPS
CIDR allowed to SSH into head and login nodes


HPC_DOMAIN, HPC_HOST
Internal host names of the login nodes (node1.<HPC_DOMAIN>, …), and the certificate domain with SSL=true


SSL
true: Workbench serves TLS itself with a self-signed *.HPC_DOMAIN certificate. false (recommended): TLS is terminated at the ALBs.


SINGULARITY_SUPPORT
Container sessions via Apptainer and the Slurm SPANK plugin. Copy your .sif images into /opt/rstudio/apptainer.


APPTAINER_VERSION
Apptainer installed on login and compute nodes when no custom AMI is used


EASYBUILD_SUPPORT
Lmod with EasyBuild modules in /opt/apps/easybuild


BENCHMARK_SUPPORT
Tiny resource profiles for load tests


LOCAL
Also offer the Local launcher on the login nodes






deploy.sh stops with an error if a Pulumi output is missing or a template contains a placeholder it can’t fill. The rendered files contain database passwords. After a real deployment they are deleted from tmp/; after --dry-run they stay there for inspection (delete them afterwards). Set KEEP_TMP=1 to keep them after a real deployment too.
When the cluster is up, ./cluster-stat.sh <clustername> prints the Workbench version, URLs and nodes. Add --show-secrets to also print the user password and the jump host SSH key.



config/cluster-config-wb.default.tmpl defines:

Head node: t3.xlarge, 120 GB root volume, runs install-pwb-config.sh as OnNodeConfigured action. ParallelCluster’s internal shared storage is on encrypted EFS.
Slurm queues, all t3.xlarge except gpu, all running config-compute.sh on start:

interactive: 1 to 5 nodes, OverSubscribe=FORCE:2, for Workbench sessions
all: 0 to 10 nodes, for Workbench jobs and batch work
gpu: 0 to 5 g4dn.xlarge nodes

Login nodes: a pool of 2 t3.xlarge instances running Workbench
Shared storage: encrypted EFS for /home and /opt/rstudio
Directory service: SimpleAD from Pulumi via LDAP, with SSH keys generated for users
Slurm accounting in the Pulumi MySQL database

config/cluster-config-wb.easybuild.tmpl is the same, plus an existing EFS mounted at /opt/apps that holds an EasyBuild software stack.
Placeholders in the templates and scripts look like @@NAME@@. To add one, use it in a template and export a matching TPL_NAME variable in deploy.sh.











Script
Runs on
When




scripts/install-pwb-config.sh
head node
OnNodeConfigured. Log: /var/log/install-pwb-config.log


scripts/config-compute.sh
every compute node
OnNodeConfigured. Log: /opt/rstudio/config-compute/<host>-<time>.log


scripts/config-login.sh
every login node
OnNodeConfigured. Log: /var/log/config-login.log



install-pwb-config.sh does the following:

Downloads the Workbench package to /opt/rstudio/scripts. Packs the session components into a squashfs image, /opt/rstudio/session-components/rsw-session-<version>.sqsh (see Section 1.5).
Writes the complete Workbench configuration to /opt/rstudio/etc/rstudio.
Writes /opt/rstudio/scripts/rc.pwb, the restart helper for the login nodes (see Section 1.6).

It touches /etc/head-node, so rc.pwb can tell the head node apart from login nodes.
config-login.sh waits for that configuration, installs Workbench, activates the license (see Licensing) and copies the configuration to /etc/rstudio. It sets the node’s www-host-name to its EC2 private DNS name, mounts /scratch and starts rstudio-launcher and rstudio-server. Finally it installs pwb-lb.sh as the pwb-lb systemd unit, which registers the node with the ALBs and cleans up after replaced login nodes (see Keeping the load balancers in sync).
config-compute.sh mounts the session components image and /scratch.



Compute nodes don’t download or extract the Workbench session components (about 800 MB as a tarball). The head node builds a zstd-compressed squashfs image of them once, on the shared /opt/rstudio EFS. Every compute node loop-mounts it read-only at /usr/lib/rstudio-server and adds the mount to /etc/fstab. This makes compute node start-up faster and guarantees that all nodes run identical session components.

The image is named after the Workbench version. Deploying a new PWB_VERSION builds a new image next to the old one.
It is written under a temporary name and then moved into place, so a node never mounts a partial image.
Compute nodes wait up to 30 minutes for the image to appear.
The mount uses threads=multi (parallel decompression) where the kernel supports it, otherwise plain ro,loop.




Login nodes copy the shared configuration only once, when config-login.sh runs. To change the configuration:

Edit the files in /opt/rstudio/etc/rstudio, so that login nodes added later get the change.
Copy the changed files to /etc/rstudio on each running login node.
Delete /opt/rstudio/workbench-<hostname>.state for each of those login nodes. config-login.sh registers rc.pwb as a cron job (every minute) on each login node, so within a minute rstudio-launcher and rstudio-server are restarted there. Its log is /var/log/rc.pwb.log.

title: Custom AMI
text:
ParallelCluster can install software when a node boots, but every minute spent installing is a minute a user waits for a session. Bringing up an EC2 instance and letting ParallelCluster configure it takes about 4 to 5 minutes. With all software baked into the AMI it stays at that; in an earlier setup that installed everything at boot time, it took more than 10 minutes.
The same AMI is used for the head node, the login nodes and the compute nodes.

title: Custom AMI
text:
3.1 R and Python
R and Python are installed from Posit’s binaries (R, Python), several versions side by side. The default version of each is symlinked into /usr/local/bin.
Each R version (configured by image/run.R):

uses the public Posit Package Manager for CRAN and Bioconductor
uses a CRAN snapshot at most 60 days newer than the R release date
has the packages needed for the RStudio IDE integration preinstalled in a site library
uses a global renv cache in /home/renv, with the renv/pak integration enabled

Each Python version:

has Jupyter / JupyterLab and the Workbench integration installed
can publish to Posit Connect (rsconnect_python, rsconnect_jupyter)
uses PyPI via the public Posit Package Manager (/etc/pip.conf)

Install logs are written to /opt/r-install.log and /opt/python-install.log in the image.
Login nodes are set up by their OnNodeConfigured action (config-login.sh), so nothing in the image is specific to login nodes. Older versions of this repository baked a cron job into the AMI for that, because login nodes did not support custom actions before. AMIs built that way keep working: the job only restarts Workbench now and never installs it.

title: Custom AMI
Custom AMI
Introduction
text:
1 Introduction
AWS ParallelCluster is a framework for setting up HPC clusters on AWS. It takes a YAML file with all the necessary definitions, transforms it into CloudFormation and deploys it. It supports Slurm as scheduler.
Posit Workbench supports Slurm as an HPC back end via the Slurm Launcher. An earlier repository showed one way to integrate the two, with Workbench running on the head node. That approach works but has several shortcomings:

The head node already runs slurmctld and slurmdbd. Adding Workbench makes it even more of a single point of failure.
All user traffic is routed through the head node.
The head node also acts as NFS server for the cluster’s shared file systems, adding load that can degrade the user experience or crash the node when resources are exhausted.

This repository documents a reference architecture that overcomes these shortcomings with a focus on high(er) availability, and contains everything needed to deploy it.


2 The approach
Several ParallelCluster features make this possible:

Login nodes (since 3.7.0). Workbench runs on a pool of login nodes behind a load balancer instead of on the head node.
Shared file systems on EFS instead of NFS exported by the head node (since 3.8.0), including /home.
Custom AMIs. When the cluster scales up, a new EC2 instance is provisioned. With all software baked into the AMI this takes about 4 minutes; installing software at boot time would make it considerably longer.

Workbench’s own state lives in PostgreSQL (required for load balancing), users come from AWS SimpleAD, and two Application Load Balancers provide TLS and DNS names. Those auxiliary services are created with Pulumi. See Architecture for the full picture.


3 Setup instructions
The deployment has three steps, each documented on its own page:

Set up the auxiliary services (VPC lookup, SimpleAD, databases, load balancers, DNS, S3 bucket, users) with Pulumi
Build a custom AMI (uses the S3 bucket and network created in step 1). You can skip this step if all sessions run in Apptainer containers; see When you need it.
Deploy the cluster with AWS ParallelCluster

If something does not work as expected, see Troubleshooting.

title: Architecture
text:
1 Overview






Figure 1: Architecture diagram



AWS ParallelCluster builds the cluster itself (head node, login nodes, compute queues and their shared storage). Pulumi creates everything around it. As much as possible lives in private subnets; only the external load balancer is exposed to the internet.








Component
Created by
Purpose




VPC with public/private subnets
pre-existing
Looked up by its Name tag (vpc_name_tag)


AWS SimpleAD
Pulumi
Users and groups for all nodes (via sssd)


AD jump host
Pulumi
Joined to SimpleAD, used to create users with adcli


PostgreSQL (pwb)
Pulumi
Workbench metadata, required for load balancing


PostgreSQL (audit)
Pulumi
Workbench audit database


MySQL
Pulumi
Slurm accounting (slurmdbd)


External and internal ALB
Pulumi
TLS termination (ACM certificate), sticky sessions to the login nodes


Route53 records
Pulumi
<stack>-ext.<domain> (external) and <stack>.<domain> (internal)


S3 bucket
Pulumi
Image build and cluster node scripts


Secrets Manager secrets
Pulumi
AD, Slurm DB and user passwords


Head node
ParallelCluster
slurmctld; writes the Workbench configuration


Login nodes (2)
ParallelCluster
rstudio-server and rstudio-launcher


Compute queues
ParallelCluster
interactive, all, gpu: Workbench sessions and jobs


EFS /home, /opt/rstudio
ParallelCluster
Home directories, shared Workbench config and data





2 Request flow
A user browses to the external ALB (https://<stack>-ext.<domain>). The ALB terminates TLS and forwards to port 8787 on one of the login nodes, using the rs-csrf-token cookie for stickiness. Workbench on the login node authenticates the user against SimpleAD (PAM/sssd) and starts sessions through the Slurm Launcher on the compute nodes. Inside the VPC, the internal ALB (https://<stack>.<domain>) serves the same login nodes. Sessions on the compute nodes use it to call back into Workbench (launcher-sessions-callback-address).
Each login node registers itself as an ALB target when it boots and deregisters itself when it shuts down. See Section 4.


3 Availability
The login nodes are managed by ParallelCluster: if one fails it is replaced, and the remaining node keeps serving users. Workbench state is in PostgreSQL and configuration is on EFS, so the Workbench part of the setup tolerates login node failures.
ParallelCluster supports multi-AZ Slurm queues, but this setup does not use them. The head node running slurmctld remains a single point of failure regardless. See Reaching full HA for ideas on how to remove it.
The RDS instances are created single-AZ and without deletion protection to keep demo environments cheap and easy to tear down. For production, enable Multi-AZ and deletion protection in pulumi/__main__.py.


4 Keeping the load balancers in sync
ParallelCluster replaces failed login nodes automatically, and the replacements get new IP addresses. To keep both the ALBs and Workbench’s own node list correct, parallelcluster/scripts/pwb-lb.sh runs on every login node as the systemd unit pwb-lb:

At boot it registers the node’s IP on port 8787 with both ALB target groups. It then cleans up:

ALB targets whose IP doesn’t belong to a running or pending login node of the cluster are deregistered.
Workbench nodes (rstudio-server list-nodes) are deleted (rserver-db delete-node) if node-status reports them unreachable and EC2 has no running login node with their IP.

At shutdown it deregisters the node from both target groups and marks it offline in Workbench (rserver-db stop-node).

The cleanup works from EC2 data, not from Workbench’s view alone. list-nodes keeps showing a node that disappeared as Online, and a node that is merely restarting can be briefly unreachable. If EC2 can’t be queried, nothing is removed. The node running the cleanup never removes itself. Logs are in /var/log/pwb-lb.log; pwb-lb cleanup can also be run by hand.


5 Licensing
Only the login nodes run Workbench, so only they need a license. The license comes from the Pulumi config (pwb_license_key or pwb_license_file). It is stored in AWS Secrets Manager (PwbLicense-<stack>), and only the login nodes can read it. On every boot, config-login.sh reads the secret:

License key: activated online with license-manager activate. Each login node uses one activation. To keep replaced login nodes from using up activations, pwb-lb deactivates the key when a node shuts down. A node that disappears abruptly can’t do that; Posit support can reset such activations.
License file: written to /var/lib/rstudio-server/license.lic. No activation or deactivation is involved, which makes it the better fit for automatically replaced login nodes.

Without a license, or if the secret can’t be read, the node runs unlicensed and logs a warning in /var/log/config-login.log. The key itself is never written to any log.


6 Storage








Mount
Type
Content




/home
EFS (encrypted)
User home directories, renv cache in /home/renv, Workbench shared storage in /home/rstudio/shared-storage


/opt/rstudio
EFS (encrypted)
Workbench config (etc/rstudio), installers and scripts (scripts), session components image (session-components), state files


/usr/lib/rstudio-server (compute nodes)
squashfs image on /opt/rstudio, mounted read-only
Workbench session components


/scratch
EFS (sub-directory of /opt/rstudio)
Scratch space bound into containers


/opt/apps
existing EFS (easybuild template only)
EasyBuild software stack



ParallelCluster’s internal shared directories (e.g. /opt/slurm) are on EFS too, so the head node does not act as NFS server.


7 Workbench configuration
All Workbench configuration is generated on the head node by parallelcluster/scripts/install-pwb-config.sh into /opt/rstudio/etc/rstudio. The login nodes copy it to /etc/rstudio when they are set up. Notable settings:

Load balancing enabled (load-balancing-enabled=1). Each login node’s www-host-name is its EC2 private DNS name, which the VPC resolves.
Two Slurm launcher clusters: slurminteractive (partitions interactive, gpu) for sessions and slurmbatch (partitions all, gpu) for Workbench jobs. With LOCAL=true the Local launcher is added.
Resource profiles sized for t3.xlarge compute nodes.
RStudio, VS Code, Positron and JupyterLab enabled.
Auditing (R console, sessions, audited jobs), monitoring and the admin dashboard (groups rstudio-admins, rstudio-superuser-admins) enabled.
Optional: Apptainer/Singularity container sessions (SINGULARITY_SUPPORT), Lmod/EasyBuild modules (EASYBUILD_SUPPORT), TLS on Workbench itself (SSL).



8 Note on SSL certificates
When you bundle certificates, put the server certificate first, followed by the intermediate certificates.

title: Pulumi
text:
Posit Workbench in a load-balanced setup needs a PostgreSQL database, and a distributed HPC cluster needs a directory service for users. This setup uses AWS SimpleAD. A small EC2 instance, the jump host, is joined to SimpleAD and uses adcli and expect scripts to create users programmatically.
The Pulumi program in the pulumi/ folder creates:

SimpleAD, plus the jump host joined to it
PostgreSQL databases for Workbench (pwb) and its audit log (audit), and a MySQL database for Slurm accounting
Secrets Manager secrets for the AD, Slurm DB and user passwords, and a secure cookie key for Workbench
An EC2 key pair, IAM policies and security groups used by the cluster
An S3 bucket for the image build and cluster scripts
An external and an internal Application Load Balancer with HTTPS listeners, plus Route53 records for both

title: Pulumi
text:
3.2 Users and passwords
Users are named positXXXX, where XXXX is a zero-padded number (posit0001, posit0002, …). They all share one password, which is generated by Pulumi and stored in Secrets Manager. You can read it with
pulumi stack output posit_user_pass --show-secrets
posit0001 additionally gets passwordless sudo on all cluster nodes.
All generated passwords are random strings of 16 characters (20 for the user password) with at least one lower-case letter, one upper-case letter and one digit. The passwords needed by ParallelCluster (AD, Slurm DB) are also stored in AWS Secrets Manager.
User creation is done by server-side-files/config/useradd.sh on the jump host. It creates up to 40 users in parallel and verifies each one with pamtester, retrying if needed.

text:

title: Pulumi
text:
3.4 Accessing the jump host
pulumi stack output private_key_ssh --show-secrets > jumphost.pem && chmod 600 jumphost.pem
ssh -i jumphost.pem ubuntu@$(pulumi stack output jump_host_private_ip)
*.pem files are ignored by git, but delete the key when you are done.

The nodes are in private subnets. Use SSM Session Manager (aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id>) or SSH from inside the VPC. ./cluster-stat.sh <clustername> lists the instance IDs.


2 Common problems
deploy.sh fails with “Pulumi output ‘…’ missing”. The stack is older than the scripts, or you are using the wrong stack name. Run pulumi up in pulumi/, and check that STACKNAME/CLUSTERNAME match the stack.
Cluster creation hangs or the head node times out. Check /var/log/install-pwb-config.log on the head node; the longest steps are the Workbench download and the session components image. Login nodes wait for the head node, so their setup only finishes after it.
Workbench URL returns 502/503. The login nodes are not (yet) healthy in the ALB target groups. Check that pwb-alb-tg-ext-<cluster> has targets (aws elbv2 describe-target-health), and /var/log/pwb-lb.log on the login nodes for registration errors. Then check /var/log/config-login.log on a login node. It waits for the head node to finish writing the Workbench configuration, so Workbench can come up several minutes after the node itself.
Sessions start but never connect. The session on the compute node can’t call back into Workbench. Check launcher-sessions-callback-address in /etc/rstudio/rserver.conf. With SSL=false it should be https://<stack>.<domain>, the internal ALB. It must resolve and be reachable from the compute nodes.
Compute nodes fail to start with “rsw-session-….sqsh not found”. The head node builds the session components image in install-pwb-config.sh; check its log for download or mksquashfs errors. On a compute node, findmnt /usr/lib/rstudio-server shows whether the image is mounted.
rstudio-server list-nodes shows nodes that no longer exist. They are removed when the next login node boots. To remove them right away, run sudo pwb-lb cleanup on a login node (log: /var/log/pwb-lb.log). Note that list-nodes shows stored state; rstudio-server node-status probes the nodes.
Workbench says it is unlicensed or the evaluation has expired. Check /var/log/config-login.log on the login node for a license warning. Run sudo /usr/lib/rstudio-server/bin/license-manager status. Is pwb_license_key or pwb_license_file set in the Pulumi stack (pulumi config)? To activate a running node by hand, run sudo rstudio-server license-manager activate <key>, or copy the .lic file to /var/lib/rstudio-server/ and run sudo rstudio-server restart.
Users cannot log in. Check that the user exists (id posit0001 on a login node) and that sssd is running. Users are created by just create-users in pulumi/, which needs SSH access to the jump host.
SimpleAD creation fails. SimpleAD needs two private subnets in different availability zones. Pulumi takes the first private subnet of each AZ, so the VPC must have private subnets in at least two AZs.
Database migration errors when Workbench starts. A Workbench downgrade, or two clusters sharing one database, can leave the pwb database in an incompatible state. Each cluster should have its own Pulumi stack (and therefore its own databases).
